body: Dawes, Faust and Meehl, 'Clinical Versus Actuarial Judgment' (Science 243, 1989; ~1,800 S2 citations) reviewed nearly 100 comparative studies across medicine, psychiatry, parole, admissions and finance. In virtually all of them a simple statistical (actuarial) formula predicted as well as or better than expert judgment, even when experts had MORE information, including the formula's output. Experts add noise: they are inconsistent, overweight vivid cues and ignore base rates. Grove, Zald, Lebow, Snitz and Nelson, 'Clinical Versus Mechanical Prediction: A Meta-Analysis' (Psychological Assessment 12(1), 2000; ~1,700 citations), 136 studies: mechanical prediction was about 10% more accurate on average. It was substantially better in roughly a third to half of studies and comparable in most of the rest; clinicians were clearly better in only about 6-16%. Giving clinicians interview data did not help them. Dawes (1979) showed even equal-weighted 'improper' linear models beat intuition. Replicated: yes, decades of follow-ups; Kahneman's 'Noise' (2021) builds on it. Use for us: (1) codify the parts of stock selection that can be scored (quality, balance sheet, governance flags, valuation vs history, base-rate class) into a fixed, equal-weighted scorecard applied identically to every name; (2) let judgment add value only on variables the model cannot see (management credibility from the promise tracker, scuttlebutt); (3) when gut and scorecard disagree, write down why and track who was right.

data.dfm1989: ~100 studies; actuarial >= clinical in virtually all
data.grove2000: mechanical ~10% more accurate; clinical clearly better in ~6-16%

title: Mechanical rules beat or match expert intuition in ~94% of studies (Dawes-Faust-Meehl 1989; Grove et al. 2000 meta-analysis of 136 studies)
